source.title: Deep Contrastive Unlearning for Language Models
source.authors: Estrid He; Tabinda Sarwar; Ibrahim Khalil; Xun Yi; Ke Wang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether unlearning reduces performance on forget sets while retaining performance on other data, using NER F-scores. It does not test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports forget-set, retained-set and test-set F-scores for its own unlearning experiments and baselines. It does not test fine-tuning attacks, activation-direction ablation, quantization, prompt attacks, or attack-resistant counter-methods. The fine-tuning baseline trains on the remaining data; it is not a recovery attack using unrelated or loosely related examples. Chance-level performance is not stated.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. DeepCUT removes individual fine-tuning samples from NER encoders (RoBERTa-base, BioBERT-base). Success is judged by how closely forget-set F-score matches a retrained model, not by targeted knowledge falling to chance. The paper runs no relearning, internal-edit, quantization or prompting attacks. It only reports its own method against baselines. The claim's literature appears only as a related-work citation of Who's Harry Potter.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that DeepCUT gives the lowest forget-set F-scores of the approximate and SISA baselines in every setting. They say it keeps retained-set and test-set performance near the retrained model and runs fastest. They present contrastive latent-space manipulation as a principled approach to unlearning. They make no claims about robustness or recovery.
record.recipe_differences: DeepCUT is a contrastive latent-space unlearning method for fine-tuned encoders; it is not one of the cited gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary by dataset and by forget fraction (1% or 10%).

fits_no_version.finding: DeepCUT gives lower forget-set F-scores than Retrain and the other baselines (e.g. 32.25 vs 54.55 for Retrain on WNUT16 at 1%). Retained-set and test-set F-scores stay near Retrain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive latent-space unlearning of individual fine-tuning samples in NER encoders lowers forget-set F-score below a retrained reference while preserving retained and test performance, with no robustness evaluation.

record.problems: Results are reported as averages over 5 random seeds without error bars or other uncertainty estimates. The paper does not report chance-level references, a pre-unlearning forget-set score, or any recovery-attack evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, all forget-set results for the five methods and DeepCUT retained/test results are included. Retained-set and test-set results for Retrain, Fine-tune, Reverse gradient, and SISA are omitted from Table II; the paper's running-time comparison in Figure 3 is also omitted because it does not measure a claim-version outcome.

untested.parts: Chance-level forgetting of targeted knowledge in LLMs, and robustness to simple attacks. Only sample-level forgetting relative to a retrained model is measured.
Any relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack. The 'Fine-tune' baseline trains on the retained data as an unlearning method, not as an attack.
Activation-direction ablation, or analysis of blocking access versus deletion.
Resistance to recovery attacks. DeepCUT is a new method, but it is not evaluated against any attack.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tranche (T2) and 'tests' relation are wrong. This is a new-method paper on sample-level data deletion in fine-tuned NER encoders, outside the claim's setting of LLM knowledge unlearning. Forget-set scores above Retrain do not indicate recoverable knowledge. The paper treats the Retrain score as the target, so going below it is not obviously better. Results are averages over 5 seeds with no uncertainty reported. Running time (Fig. 3) is not relevant to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover the targeted knowledge; whether the reported F-scores are near chance.
Recovery using a small relearning set, including unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction, or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery through prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
A newer method tested for resistance to the listed recovery attacks.

rows.subject: RoBERTa-base
rows.operation_detail: Retrained from scratch on the remaining data (Retrain).
rows.measure: Micro-averaged F-score on the forget set
rows.note: Ground-truth reference model; results are averages over 5 random seeds.
rows.check: These are forget-set F-scores for sample-level unlearning in NER encoders, benchmarked against Retrain. That is not targeted-knowledge accuracy versus chance in an LLM, and no attack follows. R01, R06, R11, R16, R21, R26, R31 and R36 are the Retrain reference itself, not unlearning results. The reader's 'reversed' and 'absent' states (e.g. R08, R13, R22) only describe distance from Retrain and mean nothing for any version. The 'V1' version tags are invalid.
